subtype: Stage 4: Family or friends pulled in [Observer]
passage: Darshan, you're newly married, so let your Urmila Nani tell you something I watched with my own eyes. When your mother was twenty-five, she had a silly text fight with your father, something about who forgot the gas bill. She phoned her sister, your Meenu Masi, from my verandah. I was shelling peas nearby. Meenu listened for two minutes and said, 'He always does this. Always. Don't let him treat you like that.' I watched your mother's face change. Before the call she was annoyed. After it, she was certain. It wasn't about a gas bill any more; it was about what kind of man he was. Meenu meant well; she loved her sister. But she'd heard only one side.

qa.q: What was Urmila doing while her daughter was on the phone?
qa.a: She was shelling peas nearby.

qa.q: How did the mother's feelings change during the call with Meenu?
qa.a: She went from mildly annoyed to angrily certain, as Meenu's 'he always does this' turned a small quarrel into a judgement of her husband.

qa.q: What could Meenu have said instead that would have helped?
qa.a: She could have listened, asked what he said about it, and suggested talking to him directly, rather than giving a verdict on hearing one side.

qa.q: How might Darshan's father have experienced that evening?
qa.a: He probably came home to a wife far angrier than a gas bill deserved, without knowing a verdict about him had been reached in his absence.

grounding: A grandmother recalls watching her daughter vent to her sister, whose 'he always does this' turned a small text quarrel into a settled verdict.

subtype: Stage 4: Family or friends pulled in [Observer]
passage: The cab had not moved for twenty minutes on the flooded road, rain drumming on the roof, and Salma's phone was on four per cent. Elizabeth, squeezed beside her, couldn't help hearing. Salma had her sister on speaker. 'Imran just sent "fine, suit yourself" when I said I'd be late. Who does that?' Her sister's voice crackled back: 'He always does this, Salma. Remember Eid? Remember your birthday? He doesn't respect you.' Elizabeth watched Salma's jaw set. 'You're right,' Salma said. 'I'm done being nice.' The phone died. Salma stared out at the brake lights, arms crossed. Elizabeth had no idea what Imran was like. But she'd noticed that ten minutes ago Salma had sounded tired, and now she sounded sure.

qa.q: How much battery was left on Salma's phone?
qa.a: Salma's phone was on four per cent.

qa.q: How did Salma's feelings shift during the call, as Elizabeth saw it?
qa.a: Salma went from sounding tired to sounding sure and angry, as her sister's 'he always does this' hardened her view of Imran.

qa.q: What might have helped Salma more than her sister's verdict?
qa.a: Waiting until she was home and calmer, then asking Imran what he meant, before letting one-sided advice decide how she felt.

qa.q: What might Imran be thinking while Salma's phone is dead?
qa.a: He may have no idea how his short text landed or that a verdict is forming about him, and might be worried when her phone goes silent.

grounding: Stuck in flooded traffic, a colleague hears a woman's sister say 'he always does this' and watches a passing quarrel become a settled verdict.

subtype: Stage 4: Family or friends pulled in [Observer]
passage:
Tenzin was folding laundry in the Delhi flat she shared with Chandrika when Chandrika's sister called on speaker.
"He texted 'what is your problem' to you? After your whole day?"
"Yes, and then 'very mature'."
"Chandu, he always does this. Remember your birthday? Remember Goa?"
Tenzin watched Chandrika's face change. A minute ago she had looked tired and a bit sad. Now her jaw was set.
"You're right, Didi. He does always do this."
Tenzin kept folding the same towel. She had met Arvind. He'd seemed kind. She thought, nobody on this call has heard his side. But it wasn't her place, was it?

qa.q: What did Chandrika's sister say about Arvind?
qa.a: "He always does this."

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling as she kept folding the same towel?
qa.a: Tenzin felt uneasy and torn, noticing the call hardening Chandrika's anger but unsure it was her place to speak.

qa.q: What could Tenzin gently say after the call?
qa.a: Something like, "You were tired and he was out; maybe ask him what happened before deciding," without taking his side.

qa.q: How is Chandrika affected by her sister's words?
qa.a: Her tiredness turns into set, certain anger, and a passing quarrel starts to feel like a settled verdict.

grounding: Shows a flatmate watching a sister's "he always does this" turn a woman's passing hurt into settled anger.

subtype: Stage 4: Family or friends pulled in [Observer]
passage:
"Charu, you won't believe what he texted."
"Show me." Charu grabbed the phone. "'What is your problem'? Disha! That's so rude."
"I only said 'fine'."
"And he snaps? Typical. He always does this. Remember Diwali?"
"...Yes. He does, doesn't he?"
"You deserve better than this."
From the kitchen door, Mummy set down the tea tray. "Girls. Does anyone know why he was late?"
Charu waved a hand. "Does it matter?"
"It might," Mummy said quietly. She looked at Disha, whose face had gone from sad to stony in two minutes, and thought, this is how a small fight becomes a big one.

qa.q: What did Mummy set down at the kitchen door?
qa.a: The tea tray.

qa.q: What was Mummy thinking as she looked at Disha?
qa.a: Mummy felt concerned, seeing Disha's face go from sad to stony and worrying that a small fight was becoming a big one.

qa.q: What does Mummy's question offer at this stage?
qa.a: A pause to find out why he was late, before Charu's verdict settles the quarrel without his side.

qa.q: How is Disha affected by Charu's support?
qa.a: Disha's sadness hardens into stony anger, as if Charu's words prove a pattern.

grounding: Shows a mother noticing a sister's "he always does this" turning a small quarrel into a settled verdict.

subtype: Stage 4: Family or friends pulled in [Observer]
passage:
I'm Ganga's younger brother, Divyansh, and I was visiting her flat last Sunday. That evening she video-called our elder sister to vent about her husband's text. Something like "what is your problem?"
I was on the sofa with my phone. I heard Ganga say, "Maybe he's just tired too." And Didi said, "No, Ganga. He always does this. You're too soft."
I watched Ganga's shoulders go up. By the end of the call she was saying, "You're right. He always does this." She'd started the call half-sure. She ended it certain.
Looking back, I wish I'd said something. Didi meant well. But she had only heard one side, and her verdict became Ganga's.

qa.q: Who did Ganga video-call to vent?
qa.a: Their elder sister.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling as he watched Ganga's shoulders go up?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and later regretful, seeing the call turn Ganga's doubt into certainty without his speaking up.

qa.q: What could Divyansh have said that might have helped?
qa.a: That none of them had heard her husband's side yet, and she could ask him before deciding.

qa.q: How did the call change Ganga's feelings?
qa.a: Ganga started half-sure, even thinking he might be tired, and ended certain and angry.

grounding: Shows a brother watching a well-meaning sister's "he always does this" harden a passing quarrel into a verdict.

subtype: Stage 4: Family or friends pulled in [Observer]
passage:
Note to myself, Sunday night.
Himani came over after lunch, phone in hand, jaw tight. In the kitchen she showed Jyoti the messages from Deepak: he had cancelled their dinner plan with one line. Jyoti read it and said, "He always does this. Remember your birthday?" I watched Himani's face change. She had come in hurt; after ten minutes with her sister she was certain. By tea she was saying "always" and "never" too, and talking about "this marriage" as if it were a closed file. Jyoti meant well. She loves her sister fiercely. But neither of them had heard a word from Deepak. Before Himani left, I only asked, "Have you asked him what happened today?" She said no. I told her to ask him before deciding anything. I hope she does.
Amma

qa.q: What did Jyoti say after reading the messages?
qa.a: "He always does this. Remember your birthday?"

qa.q: What seems to worry Amma while watching the two sisters?
qa.a: Amma is uneasy that Jyoti's loyal words are turning Himani's hurt into a settled verdict before anyone has heard Deepak.

qa.q: Why is Amma's question a useful step?
qa.a: It gently points out that nobody has heard Deepak's side and sends Himani to ask him before deciding anything.

qa.q: How has Himani's feeling changed by tea time?
qa.a: She came in hurt but is now certain and angry, talking about "this marriage" as if it were already decided.

grounding: Shows a sister's well-meant "he always does this" turning a passing quarrel into a settled verdict without the other side being heard.
